statements.text: ECR is initiated by destruction of the cementum, allowing clastic cells of the periodontium to interact with dentine; pathogenesis has initiation, resorptive and reparative phases.
In early ECR the pulp space is protected from the resorption front by the pericanalar resorption-resistant sheet (PRRS) and the pulp remains vital; ECR enters the pulp space only in advanced stages.
Aetiology is poorly understood; orthodontic treatment and a history of traumatic dental injury are the most commonly associated factors, considered predisposing rather than causative.

Early ECR is often asymptomatic and found incidentally; advanced ECR may present with gingivitis, pulpitis or periapical periodontitis; buccal/palatal lesions may show a cervical pink spot; cavitated lesions show profuse bleeding and a hard/scratchy sensation on probing.

ECR has no classic radiographic appearance: radiolucent in the resorptive phase, mottled in moderate/advanced reparative stages; borders may be well-defined or ragged; the canal outline and PRRS should remain traceable unless the canal wall is perforated.

CBCT provides essential three-dimensional information on lesion nature and extent, degree of circumferential spread and proximity to the root canal; the ESE recommends CBCT to aid diagnosis and management of ECR.
Parallax imaging and CBCT differentiate ECR from internal root resorption; internal resorption is centred on and expands the canal, ECR is eccentric with a traceable canal.

The Patel classification is a three-dimensional assessment describing lesion height, circumferential spread and proximity to the root canal; for multi-rooted teeth the total axial spread at the CEJ region and the number of roots affected determine spread.
statements.source: ESE position statement 2023; Patel et al. 2018

statements.text: Height 1: at CEJ or coronal to bone crest; 2: extends into coronal third of root and apical to bone crest; 3: into mid-third; 4: beyond mid-third. Spread A <=90, B >90-180, C >180-270, D >270 degrees. Proximity d: confined to dentine; p: probable pulpal involvement.
Treatment aims: excavate the resorptive tissue, restore the resorptive defect and monitor the tooth for recurrence.

Management depends on the nature, extent and size of the portal of entry and on the accessibility of the lesion; management options are still experimental with short-to-medium-term outcomes; prosthodontic alternatives should be discussed with the patient before treating ECR.
Posterior teeth and greater lesion extent reduce tooth survival.

Patel's management guidance: external repair for accessible lesions confined to dentine; combined external repair and root canal treatment when the pulp is involved; internal repair via the canal for inaccessible lesions; intentional replantation or extraction for extensive, inaccessible or unrestorable lesions; periodic review for untreatable but asymptomatic cases.
Cervical burnout, non-carious cervical lesions, root caries, developmental root concavities/furcation and restoration artefacts mimic ECR on CBCT; verify in multiple planes and consecutive slices.

Diagnocat's CBCT report lists per-tooth conditions with probabilities (e.g. caries signs, root caries, abfraction, periapical radiolucency, PDL widening, bone loss, endodontic treatment, restorations, internal resorption) and segments teeth, pulp/canals and jaws; it has no external/cervical resorption category.
statements.source: Diagnocat AI 4.0 user manual; JCM 2026 validation study

statements.text: In an independent CBCT validation, external resorption cases (n=14) had no corresponding Diagnocat output; the software's cleared/validated scope is other endodontic findings such as periapical radiolucency.

CDT 2024 codes used in plans: D3471/D3472/D3473 surgical repair of root resorption (anterior/premolar/molar); D3501-D3503 surgical exposure of root surface without apicoectomy or repair; D3310/D3320/D3330 endodontic therapy; D3333 internal root repair of perforation defects; D3470 intentional reimplantation; D3450 root amputation; D3920 hemisection; D7140/D7210 extraction; D0364 limited-FOV CBCT; D9310 consultation.

In a 2026 evaluation of vision-language models on radiology images, overall diagnostic accuracy was 17.3% with a 74.4% hallucination rate; adding clinical context raised accuracy (10.6% to 24.0%) but the models weighted the text more than the image. A vision-language model's opinion on a CBCT frame is therefore a weak, uncalibrated second opinion that must never replace the imaging detector or the clinician's own reading.
statements.source: Vision-language models in radiology: accuracy and hallucination (PMC12842777, 2026)

statements.text: Discrete semantic entropy over repeated samples (T=1.0) flags unreliable large-language-model answers; rejecting high-entropy outputs raised accuracy of accepted answers at the cost of coverage (e.g. 51.7% to 76.3% at 47% coverage). The system applies this selective-prediction rule to the local vision model: disagreeing samples lead to abstention and the rule-based posterior is kept unchanged.
statements.source: Discrete semantic entropy filtering for radiology LLM answers (Eur Radiol 2026)

statements.text: Two-bit weight quantization of vision-language models is lossy by design: benchmark averages drop by roughly 15% and text-in-image reading by 16 to 24 points relative to full precision. The 24 GB Nemotron 3.5 Bolt build is such a model; its outputs are treated as a down-weighted second opinion and have not been validated on dental CBCT.
statements.source: Quantization of VLMs (arXiv 2511.08914) and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt report (arXiv 2610.33039)
